newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt says only CAP prevents trade deal with EU.
newsitem.headline: Egypt says only CAP prevents trade deal with EU.

text.p: Egypt's chief negotiator with the European Union (EU) said on Monday that the only obstacle to a partnership agreement was what he called European worship of the EU's Common Agricultural Policy (CAP).

Assistant foreign minister Gamal Bayoumi told Reuters that Egypt's negotiations with the EU were "90 percent done" but both sides were still wrangling about the 15-member bloc's stand on agricultural imports.
"The EU has created a god that they pray to called the CAP which they feed every year with more than $70 billion and it has a lot of believers," he said.
"I am not asking them to change their religion, but I will keep mine. We will agree once they recognise my religion."

Egyptian and European economic experts in Brussels have been arguing over the free trade accord for years and the CAP -- which subsidises farmers within the union to increase food production -- has been at the centre of the dispute.
Egypt has repeatedly said the EU is seeking an open market for its own industrial goods but is unwilling to reciprocate on Egypt's agricultural exports.

"With the CAP, they say they are protecting three percent of the European population. We have 56 percent of the population working on agricultural land and we don't have any qualms about the free trade accord," Bayoumi said.
EU officials say that they are offering Egypt a deal similar to those accepted by Morocco and Tunisia and that they cannot make substantial amendments on the agricultural aspects.
Under a cooperation agreement reached in 1977, Egyptian and European goods already receive special advantages, but most trade has been from Europe to Egypt.

Bayoumi has said Egypt wants to increase the value of its agricultural exports to the European Union to $1 billion a year. He has not given any indication of the current value of such exports but they are only a fraction of that amount.

The European Union imposes import quotas for a wide range of agricultural products. Egypt has rarely exceeded its quota but disputes will arise in the future if Egyptian farmers start to produce large food surpluses.
